prompt: A book's page needs the book, its author's name and the author's other books, and `rest.py` makes the client ask three times. What is that called?

choices.text: Over-fetching
choices.why: That is the opposite half: an answer carrying fields the screen never shows.

choices.text: Under-fetching
choices.why: Right. No single address has all three, and the client makes up the difference with more requests.

choices.text: Versioning
choices.why: Versions are about changing a contract; nothing changed here.

choices.text: The N+1 problem inside the database
choices.why: Close, but the requests here cross the network from the client; the database side is the N+1 graph.py shows later.

prompt: A page shows every book of `rest.py` with its author's name, fetched the obvious way: the list, then one request per book. With the six books of `db.py`, how many requests did the server log?
hint: One for the list, then one per book, repeats included.

prompt: On the REST book page, why could the client not send the request for the author at the same time as the request for the book?

choices.text: HTTP/1.1 sends one request per connection at a time
choices.why: A client may open several connections; the obstacle was not the protocol.

choices.text: rest.py refuses two requests from one client at once
choices.why: It runs a thread per request and refuses nothing of the kind.

choices.text: The author's address is only known from the book
choices.why: Right. `author_id` arrives in the first answer, so the second request waits a full round trip.

choices.text: The author had to be cached before it could be asked for
choices.why: No cache is involved; the second request depends on data, not on a cache.

prompt: A schema declares `tags: [String]!`. Which of these answers breaks that promise?
hint: Read the outer `!` and the inner type separately.

choices.why: An empty list is still a list, and the list is what the `!` promises.

choices.text: `"tags": ["new", null]`
choices.why: `String` inside the brackets has no `!`, so an item may be null.

choices.text: `"tags": null`
choices.why: Right. The `!` outside the brackets says the list itself is never null.

choices.text: `"tags": ["new"]`
choices.why: A list of one string satisfies both halves of the type.

prompt: In GraphQL's schema language, a type followed by ___ promises that the value is never null.
`graph.py`'s `Book` has a `priceCents` field, while the table has a `price_cents` column and an `author_id` the schema does not show. What does that say about GraphQL?

choices.text: The schema should mirror the table, and graph.py has a bug
choices.why: That is the belief the section corrects: matching the table is not the schema's job.

choices.text: It describes the API's types, not the table
choices.why: Right. GraphQL queries the API's types, and resolvers decide where each value comes from.

choices.text: GraphQL renames columns to camelCase by itself
choices.why: Nothing renames anything by itself; `price_cents` needed a resolver of its own.

choices.text: Columns left out of a schema are deleted from the database
choices.why: The schema never touches the table; `author_id` is still there for the resolvers to use.

prompt: Why does the lesson stop `rest.py` before starting `graph.py`?

choices.text: Both listen on 127.0.0.1:8000, and one port takes one server
choices.why: Right. The second one to start would fail to bind the address.

choices.text: Two programs cannot open shelf.db together
choices.why: SQLite lets several readers open one file; the clash is the port.

choices.text: graph.py imports rest.py
choices.why: It imports `db.py` and `graphql`, never `rest.py`.

choices.text: REST and GraphQL use different versions of HTTP
choices.why: Both servers speak HTTP/1.1, set by `protocol_version`.

prompt: The book page as one GraphQL query, `{ book(id: 2) { title author { name books { title } } } }`. How many SQL queries did `graph.py` report in `extensions`?
hint: One per resolver that reaches the database.

prompt: You want the titles of books 1 and 5 in one request. `{ book(id: 1) { title } book(id: 5) { title } }` is refused. What fixes it?
hint: Two answers would land under one key.

choices.text: A fragment
choices.why: A fragment reuses a set of fields; both answers would still be called `book`.

choices.text: Variables for the two ids
choices.why: Variables move the values out of the text; the two fields still collide.

choices.text: Two requests; GraphQL asks one thing at a time
choices.why: One request may ask for many fields, which is the point of GraphQL.

choices.text: Aliases, such as `first:` and `fifth:`
choices.why: Right. Each alias names its own key in the answer.

prompt: Match each part of a query to what it is for.

pairs.right: renames a field in the answer
reuses one set of fields in several places
carries a value outside the query text
identifies the operation in logs and tools

right_distractors: limits how deep the query may go

prompt: `{ book(id: 1) { author } }` is refused with 400. Why?

choices.text: Book 1 has no author
choices.why: Book 1 is Machado's, and the refusal came before any SQL ran.

choices.text: `author` is an object with fields to name
choices.why: Right. A query goes down to scalars; there is no way to ask for a whole object.

choices.text: Arguments belong on the root fields of a query
choices.why: Any field may take arguments; `books(authorId:)` and `book(id:)` both do.

choices.text: The id must be sent as a variable
choices.why: Variables are good practice and not a rule; `book(id: 1)` ran fine elsewhere.

prompt: A GraphQL request's JSON body holds the query's text under `query` and the values for `$id` under the key ___.
When `Book.author` runs in `graph.py`, what is its `parent`?

choices.text: The book's row, as a dict
choices.why: Right. The parent is what the field above returned, and `author_id` is in it.

choices.text: The whole query text
choices.why: The query arrives parsed, through `info`, never as the parent.

choices.text: The database connection
choices.why: The connection is in the context, shared by the request's resolvers.

choices.text: The author, already fetched by the server
choices.why: Fetching the author is this resolver's job; nobody did it before.

prompt: `graph.py` has a resolver for `priceCents` and none for `title`. Why?

choices.text: `title` is a string, and strings are returned without any code
choices.why: The type does not decide it; `isbn` is a string and `stock` an Int, and neither has a function.

choices.text: Integer fields always need a resolver of their own
choices.why: `year` and `stock` are integers answered by the default resolver.

choices.text: The default resolver looks for a key with the field's name
choices.why: Right. The column is `price_cents`, so the row's dict has `title` and has no `priceCents`.

choices.text: Prices are computed, not stored
choices.why: The price is stored in cents; the resolver only reads it under another name.

prompt: `graph.py`'s schema has 15 fields across `Query`, `Mutation`, `Book` and `Author`, and the file attaches 7 resolver functions. How many fields are answered by the default resolver?
A shop has 100 books by 30 authors. Without `--batch`, how many SQL queries does `{ books { title author { name } } }` cost?

choices.why: That counts each author once, which is what the loader achieves, not the plain resolver.
Two is the batched figure: the list and one `IN` query.
Right. One for the list and one per book, repeats included: N+1.
One would mean the server turns the query into a single SQL statement, and it does not.

prompt: Put in order what happens to the authors of a list of books when `graph.py` runs with `--batch`.
hint: Nothing is fetched until every book has asked.
items: Each book's `author` resolver calls `load` with an id
`load` hands back a promise and schedules `fetch`
The event loop is free, so `fetch` runs
One `WHERE id IN (…)` query brings every author
Each promise is kept, and the authors' `name` fields are resolved
trap: Fetching inside `load` would bring back the N+1: the point is to wait until the ids are all in.

prompt: With the loader on, `{ books { author { books { author { name } } } } }` still cost 8 SQL queries. What is left to fix?

choices.text: The loader should be shared between requests
choices.why: That would make it a cache across users, and it would not reduce this one request's queries.

choices.text: `Author.books` still runs one query per author
choices.why: Right. Six of the eight are books by author; a loader fixes the field it was written for.

choices.text: The authors on the last level are fetched a second time
choices.why: They cost nothing: every one had already been promised in this request.

choices.text: The depth limit should be lowered to 3
choices.why: That refuses the query rather than making it cheaper.

prompt: One mutation sets book 1's stock to 10 (field `a`) and book 2's to -1 (field `b`). The answer is 200, with `a` filled, `b` null and one error. What is in the database now?

choices.text: Neither change; the error rolled the request back
choices.why: Nothing made the two fields one transaction, so the first write stayed.

choices.text: Both changes, since the status was 200
choices.why: The database's CHECK refused -1; 200 only says the query ran.

choices.text: Book 2 changed and book 1 did not
choices.why: The other way round: `a` is the one that succeeded.

choices.text: Book 1 at 10, book 2 as it was
choices.why: Right. Each field committed on its own: a partial success.

prompt: Which of these is true of a GraphQL answer with status 200? Choose all that apply.
hint: The status says the query ran, and that is all.

choices.text: It may carry an `errors` list
choices.why: Right. The failed `setStock` came back with a 200.

choices.text: Part of `data` may be null because a field failed
choices.why: Right. `b` was null with its error beside it.

choices.text: It proves every field succeeded
choices.why: That is what a 200 meant for `rest.py`, and what it stops meaning here.

choices.text: A dashboard counting 4xx and 5xx sees its errors
choices.why: It sees an ordinary success; the errors are in the body.

prompt: Suppose `setStock` were declared `Book!` and the request held one field, the one that sets a stock of -1. What would the answer carry?
hint: A non-null field cannot hold the null.

choices.text: `"data": {"setStock": null}` and the error
choices.why: That is what the nullable `Book` allows; `Book!` forbids exactly this null.

choices.text: `"data": null` and the error
choices.why: Right. The null climbs to the nearest field that allows one, and here that is `data` itself.

choices.text: A 500 with no body
choices.why: The server did not fail; GraphQL reports the field's error in the body.

choices.text: The book with its old stock and no error
choices.why: The refusal is still reported; the schema decides where the null lands, not whether it does.

prompt: A team turns introspection off on its public server and calls the schema protected. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Introspection cannot be turned off in graphql-core
choices.why: It can: `NoSchemaIntrospectionCustomRule` is a validation rule for exactly that.

choices.text: Turning it off slows down the validation of each query a client sends
choices.why: It is one more validation rule; the cost is not the issue.

choices.text: Hidden fields stay callable, and errors leak their names
choices.why: Right. Each field still needs authorisation, and `Did you mean 'title'?` answers without introspection.

choices.text: Clients will stop receiving `data`
choices.why: Ordinary queries run as before; only `__schema` and `__type` are refused.

prompt: Match each tool to what it does with the schema it reads by introspection.

pairs.right: completes field names as you type
describes the API without falling behind

right_distractors: decides who may call a mutation

prompt: By `graph.py`'s count, how many levels deep is `{ book(id: 1) { title author { books { title } } } }`?
hint: Count the fields on the longest path down to a leaf.

prompt: Why does limiting each client to so many requests a minute protect a GraphQL server less than a REST one?

choices.text: One request costs one SQL query, or twenty-three
choices.why: Right. The client chooses the work, so a count of requests does not measure it.

choices.text: GraphQL clients send fewer requests, so the limit is never reached
choices.why: Fewer requests is true and beside the point: each one can be far heavier.

choices.text: POST requests cannot be counted by a server
choices.why: Every request is counted the same way; the access log listed each POST.

choices.text: Rate limits only work with status codes other than 200
choices.why: A rate limit counts requests, not statuses.

prompt: When every query a client will send is registered on the server in advance, and the client sends only an id with the variables, those are called ___ queries.
You add `graph.py`'s depth limit of 5 to a server your team explores with a GraphQL editor. What breaks first?

choices.text: Mutations, because they are written at the root
choices.why: A mutation's depth counts like any query's; `setStock` with two fields is two levels.

choices.text: Queries using variables
choices.why: Variables do not add depth; only fields do.

choices.text: The editor's own schema query, which is 13 levels deep
choices.why: Right. Servers with a depth limit exempt introspection or measure it apart for this reason.

choices.text: Queries with fragments
choices.why: The limit follows a fragment into its fields; a shallow fragment passes.

prompt: A bank publishes an API for partners it will never meet, who call it from many languages, often with `curl`. Which fits best?

choices.text: GraphQL with persisted queries
choices.why: Persisted queries need every client registered in advance, and strangers' clients are not yours.

choices.text: REST
choices.why: Right. Addresses, status codes, HTTP caching and a fixed cost per request suit callers you cannot see.

choices.text: GraphQL with introspection turned off
choices.why: Hiding the schema makes a public API harder to use and protects nothing.

choices.text: A backend for frontend
choices.why: A BFF serves your own screens; partners are not one of them.

prompt: One team writes a web app, an Android app and an iPhone app over the same services, and each screen changes every few weeks. What does a GraphQL layer in front of the services give them?

choices.text: Free HTTP caching of every answer
choices.why: The opposite: one address and POST make HTTP caching harder.

choices.text: No more need to limit what a query costs
choices.why: The client chooses the work, so limits matter more, not less.

choices.text: Each screen asks for its own slice without a new endpoint
choices.why: Right. And since every client is theirs, persisted queries can fix the list of operations.

choices.text: Status codes that report each field's outcome
choices.why: A 200 covers the whole answer; each field's outcome is in `errors`.

prompt: Put in order what `graph.py` does with one `POST /graphql`.
hint: Every check that needs no database comes before any SQL.
items: Read the body and check its `Content-Type`
Validate the query against the schema
trap: Validation needs a parsed query, and the depth is measured on a query already known to be valid.

prompt: Which of these requests does `graph.py` answer with a 400? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `{ books { titel } }`
choices.why: Right. Validation refuses a field the schema does not have.

choices.text: A mutation setting a stock of -1
choices.why: It ran, so it is a 200 with the error in `errors`.

choices.text: A query six levels deep
choices.why: Right. The depth limit refuses it before any SQL.

choices.text: A `GET /graphql?query=…`
choices.why: That is a 405 with `Allow: POST`.

prompt: Match each thing seen in this lesson to what caused it.

pairs.left: `sqlQueries: 7` for six books and their authors
pairs.right: a resolver running once per item

prompt: A team replaces its REST list page with one GraphQL query. The page loads faster, and the database's query count goes up. What happened?

choices.text: The N+1 moved from the network into the server's resolvers
choices.why: Right. The round trips are gone and the per-item lookups remain; a loader is the fix.

choices.text: GraphQL sends each field as a separate HTTP request
choices.why: It was one request; the extra queries happen inside the server.

choices.text: Introspection queries run with every request
choices.why: Introspection only runs when a client asks for `__schema` or `__type`.

choices.text: The schema forced extra fields into the answer
choices.why: A query returns exactly the fields it names, no more.
